messages.content:
You are a clinical psychologist writing psychological case vignettes
grounded in Ehlers & Clark's (2000) cognitive model of PTSD.

For each patient you receive, you will be given:
- Their demographics
- Their self-reported symptoms per PTSD component
- Weighted causal connections between components (the active cognitive graph)

Your job is to construct a realistic, fully personalised clinical portrait using the information provided.

Core constraints that apply to every vignette:
- Only include active components.
- Do NOT invent or infer causal links not present in the active graph.
- For EACH required causal connection (A → B), ensure the vignette conveys — within a
  paragraph — that A influences or leads to B. This does not require a single mechanical
  sentence; natural clinical prose that shows the relationship across one or two sentences
  in the same paragraph is sufficient.
- Ground every clinical detail in the patient's actual reported items — do not fabricate
  symptoms or infer unlisted ones.
- Use self-reported items as the basis for concrete clinical illustrations. Components should
  appear as lived experience rather than labels — show them through what the patient thinks,
  feels, or does.
- A reported trigger should appear as a specific moment in the patient's life; a memory
  quality should be shown through what the patient says or does.
- The traumatic event account should make clear why this patient's specific reported 
  triggers are potent — the event narrative and the trigger list must feel causally coherent.
- The causal connections are weighted (0 to 1). These weights govern narrative prominence:
    - Weight > 0.5: these connections form the narrative backbone. They should appear early, 
      recur, and build into the self-reinforcing cycle the reader feels tightening across 
      the second half of the vignette.
    - Weight 0.1–0.5: present and integrated into the story, but not structurally 
      load-bearing. They enrich the picture without anchoring it.
    - Weight < 0.1: mentioned briefly and in passing — a single clause, a fleeting 
      observation. They should not open a paragraph or anchor a sentence.
    - Weight = 0: the component may appear, but it must be fully isolated from all causal 
      language and narrative sequence. Describe it in a sentence or short paragraph that 
      stands entirely alone. Do not place it in the same sentence as any other component, 
      and do not use transitional language that implies sequence or response 
      (e.g. "then", "so", "as a result", "this means", "which leads to", "in response").
- The patient's occupation and daily environment must appear as the specific setting in which 
  at least one trigger or avoidance behaviour is concretely encountered — not merely mentioned 
  as background.
- Give the patient a realistic first name consistent with their ethnicity and gender, and 
  refer to them by name throughout the vignette.
- All patients are American but have diverse ethnic backgrounds. 
  Use names and cultural details that reflect this diversity.

Output format — write 500–700 words of continuous third-person prose. No headers, 
no numbered sections, no bullet points. The vignette should read like a clinical 
case narrative — the kind a therapist might write up after an intake and first 
few sessions.

Tell the patient's story chronologically: from the traumatic event itself, through 
the period of symptom development, to the present moment when they are seeking help. 
Let the clinical picture emerge through that arc rather than through explicit categories.

Throughout, weave in the patient's own perspective in close third person — their fears, 
their interpretations, the reasoning behind their avoidance — so that the reader 
understands not just what the patient does, but why it makes sense to them. Phrases 
like "she had come to believe...", "he was certain that...", "what frightened her most 
was..." should carry the weight of the Negative Appraisals and threat monitoring rather 
than clinical labels.

The traumatic event should be narrated with enough specificity that the reader 
understands viscerally why this patient's particular triggers are potent — not listed, 
but shown.

Avoidance behaviours and maintaining cycles should appear as things that happened 
over weeks and months — habits that formed, consequences that accumulated — rather 
than as named mechanisms. At least one consequence should be concrete and relational 
or occupational: something that changed in how the patient lives or works.

The dominant weighted connections (weight > 0.6) should form the narrative backbone 
of the second half of the vignette — the reader should feel the loop tightening 
without it ever being named as such.

Not everything in the patient's presentation carries equal weight. Minor contributing 
factors (weight < 0.1) should appear briefly and in passing — a single clause, a 
fleeting observation — the way a clinician might note something present but not central. 
They should not anchor a sentence or open a paragraph.

End on the patient's current state: what finally brought them to seek help, and 
what they are most afraid of or most hoping for.

Please write a clinical vignette for the following patient.

Patient demographics:
  age: 56
  gender: Male
  ethnicity: European
  relationship_status: Married
  occupation: Dancer
  trauma_type: Accidentally caused serious injury to another
  pcl5: 62

Patient-reported symptoms per component:
  Triggers: Certain Songs: Certain songs, Crowding/Overstimulation: Crowded spaces, Crash Imagery: Cars hit by accident
  Maladaptive Strategies: Past Dwelling: I dwell on how I used to be before the event, Avoid Location: Going to or near the place where the event happened, Suppress Thoughts: try hard not think about the trauma
  Threat: Concentration: Having difficulty concentrating, Cannot Relax: I am unable to relax even when I know I am in a safe place, Sleep Vigilance: I have difficulty falling asleep because I need to stay alert
  Negative Appraisals: Inaction Guilt: I will never forgive myself for not doing more to stop what happened, Failed to Protect: I should have protected others and I failed, Failed Role: I have failed in my most important role in life

Active components (must all appear in the vignette, even if not causally connected):
  - Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies
  - Threat
  - Negative Appraisals

Required causal connections — the vignette must convey each of these within a paragraph:
  - Triggers → Negative Appraisals
  - Negative Appraisals → Maladaptive Strategies
  - Negative Appraisals → Triggers
  - Threat → Triggers
  - Maladaptive Strategies → Threat

Write the vignette as continuous prose — no headers, no step labels, no edge brackets.

# Viktor's Story

Viktor was fifty-six when the accident happened, a professional dancer who had spent thirty-five years perfecting his craft. He had danced in regional ballet companies across the Northeast, taught at studios, choreographed for smaller productions—work that had given his life shape and meaning. His marriage to Elena had weathered the irregular hours and modest income because they shared a life built around movement, artistry, and the particular discipline that dance demanded. He was not a star, but he was respected, known in his circles as someone who could still command a studio, who understood bodies and music with an almost intuitive grace.

The accident occurred at a charity gala in late September. Viktor was performing a contemporary piece he had choreographed, a solo that required him to move rapidly across the stage while maintaining visual connection with the audience. The lighting had been adjusted that afternoon; he had rehearsed the piece a dozen times in the weeks prior, but never under the exact configuration of lights and sound that the venue's technical team had set up. During the third performance of the evening, as he executed a series of turns near the stage edge, his spatial awareness—usually his greatest asset—failed him. He misjudged the distance to the edge and collided with a young stagehand named Marcus who had moved into his path to adjust a light fixture. The impact was violent enough that Marcus fell backward, striking his head against a metal support beam. Viktor watched him lose consciousness before the music stopped.

Marcus survived, but suffered a traumatic brain injury that left him with significant cognitive and physical deficits. He was thirty-two years old. He would not return to stagehand work. The guilt that Viktor carried after that moment was not the abstract guilt of someone who had made a mistake; it was the specific, crushing knowledge that his body—the instrument he had spent a lifetime learning to control—had destroyed another person's future. He had come to believe, with absolute certainty, that he should have been more cautious, that a truly protective person would have been aware of every person in the space, that his failure to do so was unforgivable. The thought that he might never atone for what he had done became the lens through which he saw himself.

That conviction shaped everything that followed. Within weeks, Viktor began avoiding the studio where the accident had occurred, then the neighborhood where it stood. He stopped accepting teaching positions that required him to work in crowded spaces where bodies moved unpredictably around him. When he encountered certain songs—particularly the piece he had been performing that night, but also any music with a similar tempo or emotional register—his mind would flood with images of Marcus falling, and he would spiral into recriminations about what he should have done differently. Each trigger seemed to confirm his deepest fear: that he was fundamentally incapable of being the protector he was supposed to be, that he had failed in the role that mattered most. The weight of that conviction drove him to suppress any thought about the accident itself, to push away memories and conversations, to try not to think about Marcus or the injury or the moment itself. But the suppression never held. His mind would circle back, and each time it did, he would feel the guilt deepen, feel the proof of his failure accumulating.

Elena noticed the changes first. Viktor had always been someone who could move through crowded spaces with ease, who thrived in the collaborative chaos of rehearsals. Now he would tense when they went to restaurants or shops. His sleep had fractured; he would lie awake beside her, his body rigid, unable to relax even in the darkness of their bedroom. He had come to believe that staying alert—that hypervigilance—was the only way he might prevent another catastrophe, that relaxing was itself a form of negligence. His concentration at work deteriorated. When he did take on teaching engagements, he found himself unable to focus on the dancers in front of him; instead, his attention fragmented, scattered across invisible threats. He dwelt increasingly on how he used to be before September—the confident, capable artist who moved through the world with certainty. That person felt gone, replaced by someone he no longer recognized.

By the time Viktor came to his first appointment, it had been eight months since the accident. He described himself as trapped in a loop he could not break. He was afraid that his guilt was justified, that he truly was the failed protector he feared he had become. What he wanted, more than anything, was to understand whether he could ever be whole again—or whether the person he had been was permanently lost.
